title: Sally Rooney and the problem of self-censorship
gist: Faber stopped supplying Sally Rooney's books in the UK because her pledge to donate proceeds to the proscribed Palestine Action creates terrorism-funding liability, an example of the wider chilling effect of the UK proscription on publishers, journalists and protesters.

insights.claim: Faber has stopped supplying Sally Rooney's books in the UK because it cannot pass on her UK royalties without risking criminal liability for funding Palestine Action, which she said she would donate book proceeds to.
insights.speaker: Chris Tilbury
insights.so_what: Terrorism-financing law is creating real supply constraints for UK publishers and booksellers.

insights.claim: Funding or supporting a terrorist organisation can carry a 14-year prison sentence, and Palestine Action was proscribed in the UK in July 2025 under terrorism legislation.
insights.speaker: Chris Tilbury
insights.so_what: Sets the legal exposure that drives corporate self-censorship.

insights.claim: Irish bookshops report a surge in Rooney orders from UK readers, raising untested questions about whether UK buyers could technically fall under the funding offence.
insights.speaker: Chris Tilbury
insights.so_what: Legal ambiguity may push cross-border cultural trade and create enforcement test cases.

insights.claim: The proscription has produced arrests over displaying a magazine cover and a Private Eye cartoon print-out at protests, and of journalists covering a Leicestershire protest, blurring legal lines for media.
insights.speaker: Chris Tilbury
insights.so_what: Media and publishing firms face rising legal-compliance risk and may avoid the topic.

insights.so_what: The Supreme Court ruling is the key catalyst for UK civil liberties and counter-terror law direction.

insights.claim: The author argues that legal uncertainty makes fewer publications willing to cover the issue and the public too afraid to ask questions, a self-censoring effect.
insights.speaker: Chris Tilbury
insights.so_what: Self-censorship effects can be broader than formal bans.
insights.quote: The British public has questions, but we have become too afraid to ask them.
